# Results -- Study 104 (Bollinger-Reversion) on real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py).  One recipe --
Bollinger Band lower-band pierce (20-SMA minus 2 sigma) on daily closes, enter at the
next day's open, exit at the 20-day SMA (mid-band) **or** after a fixed 20-day hold --
run across a basket of six liquid instruments and pinned against a **random-day control**
on the same instruments.  As-of **2026-06-13**; history back to 2005-01-03.
Trades pooled across the basket: **n = 811** reversion entries (~6.3/ticker/year).*

## The honest test -- lower-band entry vs random-day control (20-day time exit, gross)

A horizon-fair comparison forces both arms onto the same 20-day hold so the exit
condition does not manufacture returns for one side.  Cost = 0.

| Arm | n | win-rate | mean (bps/trade) | skew | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Lower-band reversion** | 811 | **64.6%** | **+193.09** | -0.22 | **+5.34** |
| Random-day control | 1,200 | 61.5% | +141.09 | -- | +6.20 |

- The lower-band entry earns **+193 bps/trade** gross at HAC *t* = +5.34 -- but the
  random-day control earns **+141 bps** (t = +6.20) on the **same instruments, same
  period**.  The incremental edge is **delta = +52 bps** (un-matched t ~ +0.63).
- The dominant signal is **bull-market drift** (2005-2026), not band-specific reversion.
  Both entries work because US equities drifted up ~10%/yr; a random buy-and-20-days
  almost always makes money in this period.
- **The breakout rule works just as well**: upper-band pierce earns **+118 bps/trade**
  at t = +5.49.  Both the "price returns to the bands" and the "breakout = momentum"
  folk rules are positive -- because the market went up, not because of the bands.

## Per-instrument breakdown (lower-band reversion, 20-day time exit, gross)

| Ticker | n | win-rate | mean (bps/trade) | HAC *t* | rand mean | delta |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY  | 149 | 75.8% | +140 | +1.90 | +110 | +30 |
| QQQ  | 140 | 76.4% | +226 | +3.21 | +123 | +103 |
| AAPL | 112 | 68.8% | +116 | +1.08 | +255 | -140 |
| MSFT | 119 | 78.2% | +219 | +2.86 | +93  | +125 |
| JPM  | 139 | 77.7% | +354 | +3.74 | +151 | +202 |
| XLE  | 152 | 69.1% | +105 | +1.14 | +72  | +33  |

The delta (band entry minus random) is **mixed** across instruments: positive for QQQ,
MSFT, JPM, and near-zero for SPY and XLE, and **negative for AAPL** (random beats the
band entry there, reflecting AAPL's strong secular drift that random buys capture well).

## The contradiction: the breakout rule also "works"

| Entry | n | mean (bps/20d) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Lower-band reversion | 811 | +193 | +5.34 |
| Random-day | 1,200 | +141 | +6.20 |
| Upper-band breakout | 973 | +118 | +5.49 |

All three are positive with t > 2 -- confirming the signal is the **upward drift in
the base instruments**, not a band-specific effect.  You cannot simultaneously claim
"price always reverts from the lower band" and "price breaks out from the upper band"
as two separate *band* effects; they are two ways to buy a rising market.

## Could you trade it? -- cost sweep (lower-band entry, 20-day hold)

At ~6.3 trades/ticker/year the turnover is low: round-trip costs barely dent the
gross mean.

| round-trip cost | net mean (bps/trade) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| 0.0 bps (gross) | +193 | +5.34 |
| 1.0 bps | +192 | +5.32 |
| 2.0 bps | +191 | +5.29 |
| 5.0 bps | +188 | +5.21 |

Costs are not the killer here -- the drift premium is large enough to absorb them
easily.  The problem is that the random-day benchmark absorbs the **same** drift
premium without requiring a band signal.  This makes it a **FRAGILE** strategy: it
works until the market stops trending, at which point the claimed reversion edge
may vanish or reverse.

## Synthetic positive control -- the machinery works when there's something to find

On a deterministic synthetic daily tape (`data.synthetic_daily`), the lower-band
entry recovers an advantage over random entries **only when bar-level mean-reversion
is planted**, and reads approximately 0 when it is absent (random walk):

| Planted reversion | band entry mean | random mean | band beats random? |
|---|--:|--:|:--:|
| 0.00 (random walk) | ~74 bps | ~-76 bps | yes, but by luck (t<2) |
| 0.05 | +225 bps | -24 bps | yes |
| 0.10 | +287 bps | -27 bps | yes |
| 0.20 | +344 bps | +2 bps | yes, strongly |

On the real tape the "band beats random" verdict is weak (delta t ~ +0.63), so the
real market contains only a fraction of the mean-reversion needed to make the signal
cleanly informative beyond market drift.

## Verdict

- **Signal -- WEAK.**  Gross *t* = +5.34, but the random-day control also clears
  t > 2 (+6.20), and the incremental delta vs random is t ~ +0.63 (not significant).
  The higher win-rate (64.6% vs 61.5%) is real but small; most of the gross mean is
  market drift, not band-specific reversion.  A 20-year bull-market tape inflates every
  "buy the dip" metric.
- **Tradability -- FRAGILE.**  Costs are not the issue (low turnover); the claim
  survives costs.  The problem is the benchmark: a random-day buyer does almost as
  well, so the edge is not *specifically* in the bands.  Any regime shift (bear market,
  sideways chop) could erase the drift premium the bands are merely proxying.
- **"Price always returns to the bands"? -- BUSTED.**  It is true that price returns
  to the mid-band within 20 days 64.6% of the time -- but a random buy returns to the
  mid-band 61.5% of the time.  The bands add 3 percentage points of win-rate, not a
  magic reversion attractor.  And the breakout rule is equally "valid" -- exposing both
  as just ways to play the drift.
